925.title: His death, 1839
925.hook: when he died, several queens and servants burned on his pyre, against the Gurus' teaching
925.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's funeral honestly, and point to Guru Amar Das's hymn rejecting sati as the Gurus' teaching that the court failed to follow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharani Jind Kaur, and your line was a brave queen. Which brave mother did you honor? Today is a heavy day. Go gently with it. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

The man who built the kingdom is old now. Strokes have taken much of his speech. In his last days, tradition says, he gave away gifts and treasure, and his court gathered around him in Lahore. Then the Lion of the Punjab died, and the city mourned. What happened at his funeral is part of this story, and Sikh histories tell it honestly, because the Gurus had already spoken to it. Today: his death.
screen: `THE MAHARAJA GROWS OLD.` → `HIS COURT GATHERS IN LAHORE.` → `THE LION OF THE PUNJAB DIES.`

segments.voice: First, the fact. At his cremation, several of his queens and some serving women burned with him on the pyre. This was sati, an old custom in parts of India, in which a widow died on her husband's funeral fire. Histories record it, and Sikh tellings of it are full of sorrow. Second, the Gurus. Long before, Guru Amar Das had spoken plainly. In a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, he says that women who burn themselves with their husbands' bodies are not truly called satis. The true sati, he says, is one who lives on in goodness and contentment, and honors the Lord. The Gurus spoke against the custom, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Amar Das working to end it among his followers. Third, the gap. So here is a hard thing on this stretch of the path. The kingdom ruled in the Khalsa's name, and yet at its founder's funeral, a practice the Gurus had rejected went ahead. An old custom was stronger, that day, than the Guru's word. Sikh histories say this plainly: the court fell short of the Gurus' teaching. And fourth, what to do with a hard truth. You don't have to make it smaller. You don't have to make it the whole story either. The Maharaja who gave gold to the Harmandir and mercy to his enemies is the same man at whose funeral this happened. Both are true. Holding both is part of telling history with honesty.
screen: `QUEENS AND SERVANTS ON THE PYRE.` · `GURU AMAR DAS HAD SPOKEN AGAINST IT.` · `THE COURT FELL SHORT OF THE GURU.` · `HOLDING A HARD TRUTH.` · then, large: `EVEN KINGS FELL SHORT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a hard truth. Sit, and let the breath be slow and steady. Bring to mind the women who died that day, without names, just as people. Let there be a moment of silence for them. Then, if you like, think of a hard truth in a story you love: your family's, your country's, your own. Don't argue with it. Don't hurry past it. Just let it sit beside what's good, both together. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
His death. The end of the Maharaja's life, and the funeral where queens and servants died on his pyre, against what Guru Amar Das had taught. Today's word.
Your line: even kings fell short. Today, when you see someone you admire fall short, say it plainly, and keep what was good. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

926.title: Two heirs in a year
926.hook: his son Kharak Singh sickened and died, and his grandson Nau Nihal Singh was killed by a falling arch
926.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the deaths of Kharak Singh and Nau Nihal Singh in histories of the years after Maharaja Ranjit Singh, when the Lahore throne passed quickly from hand to hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, his death, and your line was even kings fell short. Where did you see someone fall short, and keep what was good? Today, the kingdom without its founder. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

A young prince walks back from his father's cremation, through a gateway in Lahore. He's strong, clever, already a commander, the heir the court was watching. Mourners walk with him, the smoke of the pyre still in their clothes. Overhead, stones shift. The archway comes down, and the prince is struck. The kingdom that looked so solid has cremated one king that morning, and now its heir is down among the fallen stones. Today: two heirs in a year.
screen: `BACK FROM A FATHER'S CREMATION.` → `A GATEWAY IN LAHORE.` → `THE ARCH COMES DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the son. Kharak Singh, the Maharaja's eldest, took the throne. Histories describe him as gentle and not suited to the hard politics of the court. Power slipped quickly into other hands, among them his own son's and the ministers'. His favorite adviser was killed, and later Kharak Singh himself fell ill and died. Some at the time suspected poison. Nobody can say for certain. Second, the grandson. Nau Nihal Singh, Kharak Singh's son, was young, able and ambitious, and he had already been ruling in all but name. On the day of his father's cremation, as he passed under a gateway, part of it fell and struck him. He died of his injuries. Third, the doubt. Histories record the suspicion that it was no accident. Some point to the ministers who gained from his death, and say the story of what happened in the hours after was kept close. Others say the arch simply fell. The sources don't settle it, and we won't pretend they do. Fourth, what it shows. The Maharaja had spent a lifetime building a kingdom. Within a short time of his death, his son and grandson were both gone, and the throne was open to whoever could seize it. A kingdom can look like a fortress and still hang by a thread, or by the stones of one gateway.

927.title: Sher Singh and the ministers
927.hook: a new Maharaja, a court full of rivals, and a gun held out as a gift
927.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember the killing of Maharaja Sher Singh as part of the court intrigues that weakened the kingdom after Ranjit Singh, and Sikhs often point to the Gurus' warnings against falsehood when they tell it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two heirs in a year, Kharak Singh and his son, and your line was power is fragile. Where did you see something strong turn out to be thin? Today, the next man to sit on that fragile throne. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

A courtier walks across a garden toward the Maharaja, carrying a new gun. He's come, the story goes, to show it off. A fine piece, worth a look. The Maharaja reaches for it. In the histories of Lahore, that moment is where the court's long quarrel stops being whispers and becomes blood. The man on the throne is Sher Singh, a son of Ranjit Singh. The man with the gun belongs to a family he had welcomed back to court. Today: Sher Singh and the ministers.
screen: `A COURTIER WITH A NEW GUN.` → `THE MAHARAJA REACHES FOR IT.` → `SHER SINGH, SON OF RANJIT SINGH.`

segments.voice: First, the throne. After the two heirs you met yesterday, Sher Singh came to power through a hard struggle with rivals inside the royal family. He was brave and easygoing, the histories say, fond of hunting and company, and less fond of the hard, daily work of holding a court together. Second, the ministers. Around him stood the men who really ran things. Dhian Singh, the Dogra chief minister, you met at the court of many faiths. Against him stood the Sandhawalia sardars, kin of the royal house, with their own claims and grudges. Each side watched the other. Each wanted the Maharaja's ear. Third, the day it broke. The Sandhawalias had fallen out with the court and later been brought back into favor. Then, as Cunningham and other histories tell it, Ajit Singh Sandhawalia came to Sher Singh with a gun to show him, and shot him with it. The Maharaja's young son Partap Singh was killed the same day. And before the day was over, the Sandhawalias killed Dhian Singh too, the minister some accounts say had been in on the plot with them. Then Dhian Singh's son, Hira Singh, turned the army against them, and they were killed in turn. One plot, and a whole circle of men were dead. Fourth, what the Gurus had said about it. In the first pauri, or stanza, of the Japji, Guru Nanak asks how a person can become truthful, and how the wall of falsehood can be torn down. His answer is to walk in the Lord's will. Intrigue is falsehood made into a plan. It promises a safe path to power, and at Lahore it ended in a garden, a gun, and a line of graves. That's today's line.

Bring to mind one place in your life where quiet sides are forming: a group chat, an office, a family argument, a team. Notice who's talking about whom. Notice whether you've been pulled in, even a little. Now picture yourself stepping back from it, one step, not cold and not superior, just out. Breathe there for a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sher Singh, a son of Ranjit Singh, caught in a court split between rival families, and killed along with his son and his chief minister in a plot. Today's word.
Your line: intrigue kills. Today, stay out of one intrigue. When the whisper comes your way, don't pass it on. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

928.title: A child on the throne
928.hook: Duleep Singh, a small boy, becomes Maharaja, with his mother as regent
928.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Duleep Singh, enthroned as a child with his mother, Maharani Jind Kaur, as regent, and his story is told in Sikh homes and gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sher Singh and the ministers, and your line was intrigue kills. When a whisper came your way, did you let it stop with you? Today, who was left to sit on the throne. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

A small boy is led to the throne of the Punjab. His feet don't reach the floor from the cushion. Around him stand grown men who have just watched a Maharaja, a prince and a chief minister die, and who now bow to a child. Beside him, watching all of them, sits his mother. The boy is Duleep Singh, the youngest son of Ranjit Singh. The woman is Maharani Jind Kaur. Today: a child on the throne.
screen: `A SMALL BOY LED TO THE THRONE.` → `GROWN MEN BOW TO A CHILD.` → `HIS MOTHER WATCHES THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: First, why a child. After yesterday's killings, the men who held the army needed a Maharaja they could manage. Hira Singh, the dead minister's son, raised the boy Duleep Singh to the throne and ruled as chief minister in his name. A child king is easy to seat on a throne. That was part of the point. Second, the mother. Jind Kaur stood beside her son as regent, and she was no quiet figure. Histories describe her as sharp and strong-willed. Hira Singh did not last long; he too fell in the court's quarrels, and in time her own brother, Jawahar Singh, became chief minister. Third, the danger. A child can't command an army or read a treaty. Everyone around him had a plan for his name. The ministers wanted it to rule by. The army wanted it to fight under. The British, watching from across the river, wanted to know who really held the power. A boy on a throne is a name with many hands reaching for it. Fourth, how the Gurus speak of the small and the protected. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the Lord is called father and mother, kin and brother, and protector in every place, so what is there to fear? It's the safety a small child feels when someone greater is watching. Duleep Singh had a throne, a mother and a court. What he needed most was someone who wanted nothing from him. That's today's line.

929.title: The soldiers' councils
929.hook: the Khalsa army elected councils and grew powerful as the court weakened
929.howItsDone: Sikh histories describe how the Khalsa army's regimental panchayats grew powerful after Ranjit Singh's death, and Sikh tradition still values decisions made together in the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child on the throne, young Duleep Singh, and your line was a child king. Which child did you look out for? Today, the men in the camps outside the palace, and what they did while the court quarreled. Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

Evening in a regimental camp outside Lahore. The cooking fires are lit. A group of soldiers sits in a circle, men chosen by their comrades to speak for them. They aren't talking about drill. They're talking about the court: which minister is honest, which one owes them pay, and what the regiment should do about it. Across the city, the men in the palace are starting to worry about circles like this one. Today: the soldiers' councils.
screen: `A CIRCLE BY THE COOKING FIRES.` → `MEN CHOSEN BY THEIR COMRADES.` → `TALKING ABOUT THE COURT.`

segments.voice: First, the councils themselves. After Ranjit Singh, as the court fell into plots and killings, the regiments of the Khalsa army began to choose councils from their own ranks. Histories call them panchayats, the old Punjabi word for a village council. The councils spoke for the soldiers, kept order among them, and more and more, spoke to the court. Second, the name they used. The army began to speak of itself as the Khalsa, the Guru's own body of the initiated, and not only as the Maharaja's troops. Cunningham, a British officer who wrote a history of the Sikhs, describes the army in these years as seeing itself as the true voice of the Panth. That's a big claim for soldiers to make, and the court felt its weight. Third, what the councils did. They pressed for pay. They backed one minister and turned on another. When Jawahar Singh, the Maharani's brother, was blamed for the death of a prince, the army called him before its councils, and he was killed by the soldiers. The court had lost the power to command its own army. The army had become a power of its own. Fourth, the two sides of it. Some Sikh tellings hear an older echo in these circles: ordinary men refusing to be only tools of the powerful. The Gurus sat with the sangat, the congregation, and Sikh tradition values decisions made together. But an army that rules a court is a dangerous thing, and its leaders could be flattered and steered. The councils gave the soldiers a voice, and the voice grew louder than anyone could control. That's today's line.

930.title: The Samadhi in Lahore
930.hook: his memorial stands beside Lahore Fort, near a gurdwara
930.howItsDone: Sikh pilgrims who travel to Lahore visit Gurdwara Dera Sahib, the place of Guru Arjan's martyrdom, and the Samadhi of Maharaja Ranjit Singh beside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soldiers' councils, which claimed to speak for the Panth, and your line was the army spoke. Whose voice from lower down did you hear? Today we step out of the noise of the court and into a quiet building of stone. Day nine hundred thirty.

Stand in old Lahore with your back to the great walls of the Fort. In front of you rises a pale building with a gilded dome and small domes around it, and arched windows of carved stone. Next to it is a gurdwara. Nearby, the huge red mosque of a Mughal emperor. Inside the pale building, under a canopy, are urns of ashes. This is where the Maharaja who took Lahore came to rest. Today: the Samadhi in Lahore.
screen: `A PALE BUILDING BY THE FORT.` → `A GURDWARA NEXT DOOR.` → `URNS OF ASHES UNDER A CANOPY.`

segments.voice: First, the word. A samadhi, in the Punjab, is a memorial raised over the place where a person was cremated. It isn't a tomb in the usual sense, since there's no body, only ashes and memory. Ranjit Singh's samadhi was begun after his death by his son, and finished in the years of the troubles you've been hearing about. Second, the neighbor. Right beside it stands Gurdwara Dera Sahib, which marks the place where Sikh tradition says Guru Arjan, the Fifth Guru, was martyred in Lahore. So the Maharaja's memorial stands next to the memory of a Guru who gave his life. The two buildings share one courtyard of memory. Third, the Guru's word. Sikh tradition links Guru Arjan's last days in Lahore with a line from one of his own hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib: what you do seems sweet to me, and Nanak asks only for the treasure of the Name. A king's memorial of gold and stone stands beside the memory of a Guru who asked for nothing but the Name. And inside the samadhi, small memorials keep the queens and serving women who died on his pyre, the sorrow from five days ago, close beside him. Fourth, what a memorial does. It keeps a name in one place, so people can come and stand before it. Sikhs from across the border still visit when they can. The building can't tell you everything about the man. But it gives the memory an address. That's today's line.

931.title: How the kingdom is remembered
931.hook: Sikhs remember it with pride and also discuss its failings
931.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the kingdom of Maharaja Ranjit Singh with pride in songs, paintings and family stories, and Sikh writers and teachers also discuss its failings openly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Samadhi in Lahore, and your line was remembered in stone. Whose name did you read all the way through? Today, memory that isn't made of stone, and we close the week. Day nine hundred thirty-one.

A family dinner somewhere in the Punjab, or in Toronto, or in Birmingham. A grandfather is talking about Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the Lion of the Punjab, and the time when a Sikh flag flew over Lahore. His granddaughter has been reading too. She asks about the court's killings, the queens on the pyre, the ministers who sold each other out. For a moment the table goes quiet. Then the grandfather nods. Both of them are telling the truth. Today: how the kingdom is remembered.
screen: `A GRANDFATHER AND THE LION OF THE PUNJAB.` → `A GRANDDAUGHTER'S HARD QUESTIONS.` → `BOTH ARE TELLING THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: First, the pride. For many Sikhs, the kingdom of Ranjit Singh is a time when the Khalsa that had been hunted ruled in its own name. The Harmandir shone with gold. Coins carried the Gurus' names. A court of many faiths served one Maharaja, and mercy was part of his memory. Songs, paintings and family stories keep that alive. Second, the failings. Sikh writers and teachers also talk openly about what went wrong. The Maharaja was rebuked at the Akal Takht for his own conduct. His court was full of rivals. After his death, plots killed his heirs and ministers, and the army grew louder than the throne. And the queens and servants who died on his pyre are part of the story too. Third, why the Gurus make room for both. In a hymn of Guru Nanak in Sri Rag, he says truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living. That sets a hard standard for remembering. A memory that only boasts isn't fully true. A memory that only blames isn't either. Fourth, the week. Look back at the road this week: the Maharaja's death, two heirs lost in a year, Sher Singh and the ministers, a child on the throne, the soldiers' councils, a samadhi of stone, and now this. It's been a hard week of the story. Holding pride and honesty at once is how a community keeps a kingdom without pretending about it. That's today's line.
screen: `THE PRIDE: THE KHALSA RULED.` · `THE FAILINGS, SAID OPENLY.` · `TRUTHFUL LIVING, HIGHER STILL.` · `A WEEK OF A HARD STORY.` · then, large: `PRIDE AND HONESTY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes holding both. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind something you belong to and care about: a family, a town, a team, a country, a community. First, let one thing you're proud of come forward. Rest with it for a few breaths. Then, gently, let one honest failing come forward too. Don't push the pride away to make room. Let them sit side by side, like two people at the same table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sach, truth. Guru Nanak says truth is higher than everything, and truthful living higher still, the standard for remembering a kingdom honestly. Today's word.
Your line: pride and honesty. Today, when you talk about something you love, name one thing it got wrong as well. Day nine hundred thirty-one.
